As an example of the CLT in practice, see Fig.\ \@ref(fig:CLTDemoLatex), where samples of various sizes are taken from a $\text{Gamma}(2, 1)$ distribution, which is very right-skewed.
The sampling distribution of the sample mean appears more like an approximate normal as the sample size gets larger, and the approximation is reasonably good even for $n = 10$.



```{r, CLTDemoLatex, fig.align="center", echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Exact sampling distribution of the mean (solid lines) overlaid with the asymptotic CLT normal approximation (dashed lines). The samples are drawn from a Gamma$(2, 1)$ distribution.", out.width='100%', fig.width=7}
# Gamma(alpha=2, rate=1): Xbar ~ Gamma(n*alpha, rate=n)
# mu = 2, sigma = sqrt(2)

###  Set up  ###
alpha <- 2
beta  <- 1
mu    <- alpha / beta
sg    <- sqrt(alpha) / beta


ns <- c(1, 2, 10, 25, 50, 100)

###  Build x grid and densities for each n  ###
traces <- lapply(ns, function(n) {
  se   <- sg / sqrt(n)
  x    <- seq(max(mu - 5*se, 1e-4), 
              mu + 5*se, 
              length.out = 600)
  yex  <- dgamma(x, 
                 shape = n * alpha, 
                 rate = n * beta)
  yclt <- dnorm(x,  
                mean  = mu,        
                sd   = se)
  list(x = x, 
       yex = yex, 
       yclt = yclt, 
       n = n)
})

###  Build figure  ###
par(mfrow = c(2, 3),
    mar = c(5.1, 3.1, 4.1, 1.1) ) # DEFAULT: 5.1 4.1 4.1 2.1

for (i in (1:length(ns))){
  plot(x = traces[[i]]$x, 
       y = traces[[i]]$yex,
       type = "l",
       xlab = expression(bar(italic(X))),
       ylab = "",
       axes = FALSE,
       main = expression(bold(Sampling~distribution)),
       sub = bquote("(" * Sample~size~italic(n) == .(ns[i]) * ")"),
       lwd = 2)
  axis(side = 1)
  lines(x = traces[[i]]$x, 
        y = traces[[i]]$yclt,
        lty = 2,
        lwd = 2)
}
```
